The nestling phase is brief, and by the time a chick achieves its first flight, it has more than doubled its birth mass significantly, although it still has substantial somatic growth ahead. The period between achieving sexual maturity and initiating a first brood likely allows the juvenile to accumulate sufficient foraging experience and fat reserves to sustain the energetic demands of egg production and subsequent parental care. Delayed first breeding is a common strategy among caprimulgids, which face unpredictable insect prey availability and must time their reproductive efforts to coincide with peak food abundance.

Adult body mass in the Eastern whip-poor-will exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a pattern documented across many caprimulgid taxa. The discrepancy between male and female asymptotic masses is consistent with the general pattern observed in species where females invest heavily in single large eggs relative to their body size.
